objectives: Distinguish recession types (demand vs supply vs financial).
Reason about Great Depression + Great Recession + COVID.

slides.title: Business cycles + recession
slides.body:
**Business cycle**: recurrent fluctuations in aggregate economic activity around long-run trend.

Four phases (NBER definition):
• **Expansion**: rising employment + output + spending.
• **Peak**: turning point; high.
• **Contraction / recession**: falling activity for ≥2 consecutive quarters (rule of thumb).
• **Trough**: turning point; low.

**NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee** (US): committee of academic economists declares peaks + troughs based on:
- Employment.
- Real personal income excluding transfers.
- Real consumer spending.
- Industrial production.
- Manufacturing + trade sales.

NBER definition more comprehensive than '2 quarters of GDP decline' which is journalists' shorthand.

**Recent US recessions**:
- 1990-91: 8 months (oil shock + S&L crisis).
- 2001: 8 months (dotcom bust + 9/11).
- 2007-2009: 18 months — 'Great Recession.'
- 2020 Feb-Apr: 2 months (COVID, deepest + shortest).

**Variables that move**:
- Pro-cyclical (rise in expansion): GDP, consumption, investment, employment, hours worked, inflation often.
- Counter-cyclical (rise in recession): unemployment, bankruptcies, defaults, government deficit, savings rate.
- Leading indicators (anticipate cycle): yield curve (inversion → recession risk), housing starts, stock market, building permits, manufacturers' new orders, ISM PMI, consumer expectations.
- Coincident: payrolls, industrial production, real income.
- Lagging: unemployment rate, prime rate, average duration of unemployment.

**Composite leading indicator (Conference Board LEI)** + similar combine multiple signals; predicts recession ~6-9 months ahead with moderate accuracy.

**Inverted yield curve** (3-month vs 10-year Treasury): historically reliable recession predictor (lead ~6-24 months). 2022-2024: inverted for record duration but no recession (yet).

slides.title: Causes of recessions: demand vs supply vs financial
slides.body:
**Demand-driven recessions**: AD shock (Keynesian).
- Consumer + business confidence falls.
- Income falls → spending falls → more income falls (multiplier).
- Inventory adjustments amplify.
- Examples: 1973-75 (oil + tightening); 1990-91 (S&L + oil); 2001 dotcom.
- Policy response: expansionary fiscal + monetary.

**Supply-driven**: AS shock.
- Oil shocks 1973, 1979, 1990, 2022.
- Pandemic supply chains 2020.
- Result: stagflation (inflation up, output down).
- Policy harder: ease + risk inflation; tighten + worsen recession.

**Financial recessions**: credit crunch + balance-sheet deleveraging.
- 2008-09: housing bubble + subprime + Lehman + global crisis.
- 1929-33 Great Depression: banking panics + monetary collapse.
- 1990 Japan: real-estate + equity bubbles + 'lost decades.'
- Recovery slow + long; balance-sheet repair time.
- Policy: aggressive monetary + fiscal + financial stabilization.

**Geopolitical + war-related**:
- 1917-19 (WWI demobilization).
- 1945-46 (WWII demobilization).
- 1990-91 (Gulf War).
- 2022-23 (Ukraine war + commodities).

**Pandemic 2020**:
- Combined supply (lockdowns reducing production) + demand (consumer pullback) + financial (rapid liquidity crisis briefly).
- Massive fiscal response (~$5T US; equivalent globally).
- Fed QE + facilities.
- Recovery rapid (V-shape) but uneven.

**Modern era characteristics**:
- Recessions less frequent + shorter than 19th century.
- Inflation-targeting + macroeconomic policy → smoother cycles.
- Asset-price + financial cycles longer + more prominent.
- Global integration → more synchronized cycles.
- Climate + supply-chain shocks may rise.

slides.title: Three notable recessions: 1929, 2008, 2020
slides.body:
**Great Depression 1929-1939**:
- Trigger: Black Tuesday Oct 29 1929 stock crash; ~89% S&P decline by 1932.
- Banking panics 1930-33: ~9000 banks failed; deposit insurance ne'er.
- Money supply collapsed (Friedman-Schwartz; Bernanke).
- Gold standard constrained policy.
- Smoot-Hawley tariff worsened trade.
- Real GDP fell ~30% peak-to-trough; unemployment 25%; deflation 25% cumulative.
- Recovery: WWII demand + monetary expansion (post-1933 gold standard abandonment).
- Causes: monetary contraction (Friedman-Schwartz), debt-deflation (Fisher 1933), expectations (Keynes), structural (Galbraith).
- Lessons: deposit insurance (FDIC 1933), Fed lender-of-last-resort, fiscal stabilization, Bretton Woods institutional framework, importance of inflation expectations.

**Great Recession 2007-2009**:
- Trigger: housing-bubble burst + subprime mortgage crisis; Lehman Sept 2008.
- Financial system frozen; trust collapsed; global contagion.
- Real GDP fell ~4.3% US; unemployment 10%; trillions in wealth destroyed.
- Policy response: Fed unprecedented (QE1-3, facilities, AIG bailout, TARP); ECB SMP; coordinated.
- Recovery slow: balance-sheet repair, household deleveraging, housing market.
- Causes: shadow-banking + leverage + securitization + credit-default-swaps + housing bubble + regulatory failure.
- Lessons: macroprudential regulation (Dodd-Frank, Basel III); stress tests; financial-stability mandate; lender-of-last-resort broader scope; international coordination (G20).

**COVID Recession Feb-Apr 2020**:
- Trigger: pandemic + lockdowns.
- Real GDP fell ~10% Q1+Q2; unemployment spiked to 14.7% in April.
- Sharp + short: 'V-shape' recovery rather than 'L-shape'.
- Policy response: $5T US fiscal (CARES, ARP); Fed massive QE + facilities; coordinated globally.
- Recovery rapid but uneven; supply chains, labor markets, sectors.
- Caused 2021-23 inflation surge from demand-supply mismatch.
- Lessons: rapid response works; fiscal + monetary coordination; resilience + redundancy in supply chains; remote work + digital economy.

Each recession reshaped institutions + policy. Modern macro = product of these lessons.

question.question: Trace COVID recession + policy response
question.goal: Walk through 2020 COVID recession + the historic policy response.

steps.prompt: When did US recession officially begin + end (NBER dates)?
steps.reveal: **NBER dated US recession**: peak Feb 2020 → trough April 2020. Total: 2 months. Shortest US recession in history.
Q2 2020: real GDP fell -8.9% (annualized -32%). Unemployment Feb 3.5% → April 14.7% (record). ~22M jobs lost in March-April.

**CARES Act** (Mar 2020): $2.2T. Includes:
- Direct payments ($1200 + $500).
- PPP small business loans + grants ($350B + $310B more).
- Expanded UI ($600/wk).
- Industry relief + Fed lending.
**Consolidated Appropriations Act** (Dec 2020): $900B more.
**American Rescue Plan** (Mar 2021): $1.9T.
Total: ~$5T US fiscal response 2020-21. Largest in history both nominal + as % GDP.

**Fed response (March 2020)**:
- Cut FFR from 1.75% to 0-0.25% in 2 emergency moves.
- Announced unlimited QE.
- 9 emergency-lending facilities: Primary Dealer, Money Market Mutual Fund, Commercial Paper, Main Street Lending Program, Municipal Liquidity Facility, etc.
- Balance sheet: $4T → $7T → $9T peak in 2022.
- Coordinated international (currency swap lines).

**Recovery**:
- GDP recovered Q4 2020 to pre-pandemic peak.
- 'V-shape' rather than 'L-shape' worst-case.
- Unemployment dropped to 3.6% by Apr 2022.

**Inflation surge 2021-23**:
- Stimulus + supply chains + commodities → demand-supply mismatch.
- CPI peaked 9.1% (Jun 2022).
- Fed pivoted from accommodation to tightening 2022.

**Lessons**:
- Rapid + decisive policy works.
- Coordination across fiscal + monetary key.
- Pandemic supply chains created lasting policy lessons.
- Modern policy frameworks can handle major shocks.

question.question: Drag to the duration (in months) of the COVID recession (Feb-Apr 2020).
question.explanation: COVID recession: 2 months (Feb 2020 peak → Apr 2020 trough). NBER-dated shortest US recession ever. Sharpest + deepest in modern era — GDP fell -10% in Q1+Q2; unemployment 14.7%. Recovery rapid (V-shape). Historically: Great Recession 18 months (2007-09); Great Depression 43 months (1929-33). Modern recessions ~6-18 months typical.

question.question: Classify each recession by its primary cause.
question.explanation:
Recession-cause classification:
• **Demand-driven**: Volcker 1981-82 (deliberate Fed tightening to break inflation); 2001 dotcom (asset-price bust + 9/11 confidence). Treatable with fiscal/monetary stimulus.
• **Supply-driven**: 1973-75 OPEC oil embargo. Difficult — stimulus risks inflation.
• **Financial / banking**: Great Depression 1929-33 (banking panics + monetary collapse + gold standard); 1990-91 S&L crisis; 2007-09 Great Recession (housing bubble + Lehman); Japan 1990s (real-estate + equity bubbles + balance-sheet recession). Recoveries long; require aggressive financial-system stabilization + restructuring.
• **Geopolitical / pandemic**: 2020 COVID (combined supply + demand shock; sharp + short); 2022-23 Ukraine impact (commodity shock).

Most recessions have multiple causes; classification reflects dominant trigger.

question.question: Why has the US not had a recession from 2020-2024 despite Fed rate hikes 0 → 5.5%?
options: Multiple supporting factors: (1) strong consumer balance sheets from COVID stimulus + housing-equity gains; (2) labor market resilience — companies hoarded labor; immigration helped; (3) inflation cooling without unemployment rising significantly; (4) fiscal stimulus + Inflation Reduction Act + CHIPS Act provided demand even during tightening; (5) financial system more resilient post-Dodd-Frank; (6) inflation expectations remained anchored. Soft-landing largely achieved despite many predictions of inevitable recession. Fed's 2022-24 disinflation may be classic case of model success.
question.explanation:
**US 2022-2024 'soft landing' factors**:

*Why no recession despite aggressive tightening*:

1. **Strong consumer balance sheets**:
   - COVID stimulus left households with high savings + low debt.
   - Housing-equity gains: HOLDER equity from rising home prices.
   - Stock-market gains + retirement savings.
   - 'Excess savings' from 2020-21 estimated $2.5T.

2. **Labor market resilience**:
   - Companies 'hoarded' labor after COVID hiring difficulties.
   - Unemployment stayed 3.5-4% throughout.
   - Wage growth real but not spiraling.
   - Demographic shifts (retirements + lower fertility) supported tightness.

3. **Immigration**:
   - Surge in 2022-23 helped supply labor + cool wage growth.
   - Crucial for sectors like construction + services.

4. **Inflation cooled supply-side**:
   - Supply chains healed.
   - Energy prices fell.
   - Goods deflation in 2023-24.

5. **Fiscal stimulus**:
   - Inflation Reduction Act (Aug 2022): $700B over decade for climate/health/tax.
   - CHIPS Act (Aug 2022): $52B semiconductor manufacturing.
   - Bipartisan Infrastructure Law (2021): $1.2T over 10 yr.
   - Combined: substantial demand support during Fed tightening.

6. **Financial system resilience**:
   - Post-Dodd-Frank stronger capital + liquidity.
   - Even SVB + Signature failures March 2023 contained quickly via SVB resolution + BTFP.
   - No broader financial crisis.

7. **Anchored inflation expectations**:
   - 5Y forward expectations stayed ~2-3%.
   - Households + firms didn't go into wage-price spiral.
   - Critical for soft landing.

8. **Productivity surge possibilities**:
   - Some evidence of post-pandemic + AI-driven productivity.
   - Reduces inflationary pressure of any given output growth.

9. **Fed framework + communication**:
   - Clear forward guidance.
   - Transparent dot plots.
   - Avoided 1970s-style policy lag.

10. **Soft-landing precedents**:
    - 1994-95 + 1984-85 cycles: similar tight + soft-landing pattern.
    - 2024 echoes these.

*Counter-arguments + caveats*:

- Recession risk not over; long + variable lags in monetary policy.
- Some 'recessions of part of economy' (commercial real estate, regional banks).
- Sectoral pain: manufacturing weak; tech layoffs.
- Recession could still arrive in 2025-26.

*Models that predicted recession*:
- Yield-curve inversion (record duration since 2022).
- Leading economic indicators (LEI) declining.
- Sahm Rule (unemployment rise from low) triggered in some readings.
- Most pre-2024 forecasts: 60-80% probability of recession.

*Models that predicted soft landing*:
- Fed staff models.
- Some private forecasters.
- Argument: 2020+ economy different from past — different to use historical recession indicators.

*Lessons*:

1. **Disinflation without recession is possible**: maybe rare but not impossible.
2. **Model uncertainty**: even sophisticated models miss regime changes.
3. **Credibility + clear communication matter**: 2022-24 Fed delivered.
4. **Combined stimulus + monetary tightening**: unusual; offsetting effects.
5. **Recession-indicator caveats**: yield-curve + LEI may need recalibration.

*Modern view*:
US achieved (so far) what was widely thought impossible: bringing inflation from 9% back to ~2.5% without significant recession or unemployment rise. Whether 2025 brings delayed recession or continued soft landing is open question.

Macroeconomic models + Fed framework + lessons from past episodes all contributed; the outcome may be replicable but requires anchored expectations + flexible labor markets + fiscal support.

slides.workedSolution: US 2022-24 soft landing factors: strong consumer balance sheets (COVID savings), labor-market resilience (hoarding, immigration), inflation cooled supply-side (chains, energy), fiscal stimulus (IRA, CHIPS, BIL), financial-system resilience (Dodd-Frank), anchored expectations, productivity surge possibilities, clear Fed framework. Disinflation without major recession; widely predicted recession didn't arrive. Lessons: model uncertainty, credibility matters, combined fiscal-monetary effects, recession-indicators need recalibration. 2025+ uncertain.

question.question: US 2020: GDP fell 8.9% (annualized) in Q1; +9.4% in Q3; +4.5% Q4. By how much (in % cumulative) did GDP change from Q1 to Q4? (Approximate cumulative.)
question.hint: Q1 -8.9%, Q3 +9.4%, Q4 +4.5%. Cumulative approximately -8.9 + 9.4 + 4.5 ≈ +5%. Recovery exceeded the initial decline by end of 2020.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain how the 2008 Great Recession reshaped US monetary + fiscal policy + financial regulation.
question.rubric: Mentions: 2007-09 Great Recession triggered comprehensive reforms. Monetary: Fed deployed unprecedented QE1-3, expanded balance sheet 4×, forward guidance, near-zero rates 7+ yr, ZLB toolkit. Fiscal: ARRA 2009 $800B, auto bailout, Fed swap lines. Regulation: Dodd-Frank 2010 (largest financial reform since 1930s) — CFPB consumer protection, Volcker rule, derivatives via central clearing, FSOC systemic-risk oversight, stress tests, capital + liquidity requirements (Basel III), living wills + resolution authority. Macroprudential: Federal Open Market Committee considers financial stability; SCAP/DFAST stress tests annual; counter-cyclical capital buffer. International: G20 became key policy coordination forum; FSB (Financial Stability Board) emerged. Lessons institutional: independent central banks need broader mandates beyond inflation; financial stability is monetary concern; international coordination essential. Theoretical: Bernanke + Yellen + Powell legacy. Concludes: reshaped global financial architecture for 2010s-2020s.
